summary:
Algeria criminalises same-sex conduct. The operative provision is the Penal Code of 1966 (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966), which ILGA records as covering both male/male and female/female relations with penalties of two months' to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. The US State Department's 2023 country report gives the same range for undefined "homosexual acts", and the UK Home Office country-of-origin information report of 26 July 2026 confirms the 1966 code remains in force, citing Human Dignity Trust material updated in June 2026.

There is no legal route to gender recognition. Cairo 52 reports that no legal framework exists for gender-affirming healthcare, that the absence of any recognition procedure blocks civil-status gender-marker changes in practice, and that Penal Code articles 274 and 264 could be deployed against healthcare providers, amounting to de facto criminalisation of transition-related care. A Snopes fact-check published on 5 August 2024 rated as true the claim that Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and prohibits being transgender.

Enforcement is documented but poorly characterised as to gender identity. Cairo 52 reports arrests within the LGBT+ community in which little information is available on whether those detained were transgender. In the clearest recorded case, a police raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province on 24 July 2020, over an alleged "gay wedding" led to the arrest of 44 people (9 women and 35 men, mostly university students); on 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and gave 42 suspended terms, relying on party decorations and the defendants' "gay appearance" as evidence.

Detention carries additional exposure. The US State Department reports that prison authorities separate vulnerable detainees, but that LGBTQI+ prisoners have no specific legal protections, and that civil society documents compounded discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office report of 26 July 2026 assesses internal relocation within Algeria as viable for gay men but finds that lesbians and transgender women face significant societal difficulties, indicating a narrower margin of movement for trans people than for gay men.

The same report sets the current asylum-authority baseline for Algeria: refusals of claims from the country are rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded, a standard relevant to anyone weighing onward protection options.

Regional polling by the Arab Barometer (BBC, 23 June 2019; about 25,000 respondents across ten countries plus the Palestinian territories) identified Algeria as the exception where fewer than half of respondents would accept a woman as head of state, one indicator of the conservative social environment in which trans visibility is punished informally as well as by law.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same Penal Code of 1966 that governs visitors, with imprisonment and fines for same-sex conduct and no statutory protection for LGBTQI+ detainees.

For resident transgender people the practical position is a closed loop: no recognition procedure means civil-status documents cannot be corrected, and the absence of any legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare means transition-related care is unavailable through lawful provision, with clinicians exposed under Penal Code articles 274 and 264.

Arrest records compiled by NGOs do not identify the gender identity of those detained, so the number of transgender people processed through the criminal justice system is not established. Civil society reports compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons, and lesbians and transgender women are assessed as facing greater difficulty relocating internally than gay men.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved on the sources reviewed: no material addresses border or visa screening, document inspection, entry refusal grounds, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, or recognition of foreign marriages or partners for Algeria. Whether articles 274 and 264 have actually been used in prosecution of healthcare providers is not sourced; the claim is that they could be.

Penalty figures from ILGA date to a 2008 edition of State-Sponsored Homophobia and the range is corroborated by the US State Department's 2023 report and by the 2026 UK Home Office review, but no source in the inventory reports a case-by-case survey of fines actually imposed. The 2020 Constantine Province convictions are the single detailed enforcement record available; national arrest totals by year are not sourced.
